LEARN MORE » Sections বাংলা Monday, November 23, 2026 Today's Paper Video e-Paper Second Edition Contact Sections Home Frontpage Asia City World OP-ED Editorial Business Global Business Commercial Capital Sports Countrywide Featured Sex & Relationship Student Voice LitScape Life Style Reciprocal Teens & Twenties In Vogue Food & Nutrition Bookshelf Entertainment Back Page × Home World Published: 10:23 PM, 21 November 2026 Ethiopia, Sudan Accuse One Another of Backing Armed Groups AA News Desk Tensions between Ethiopia and Sudan have escalated sharply as the two neighboring countries accuse each other of supporting armed groups fighting within their respective territories. The growing diplomatic dispute has raised fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa, a strategically important region already struggling with political instability, civil wars, humanitarian emergencies, and competing regional interests. Analysts warn that continued hostility between Addis Ababa and Khartoum could transform their internal conflicts into a dangerous regional confrontation. The latest tensions have emerged against the backdrop of Sudan's devastating civil war, which began in April 2023, and renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Both countries have accused the other of providing assistance to armed opponents, including military training, logistical support, access to territory, and other forms of cooperation. However, both governments have rejected the allegations made against them, and the claims have not been independently verified. Sudan's military leadership has accused Ethiopia of allowing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), to establish camps on Ethiopian territory. According to Sudanese officials, Ethiopian territory has allegedly been used to facilitate drone operations and cross-border attacks against Sudanese positions and infrastructure. Khartoum considers such activities a direct threat to its national security and territorial sovereignty. In early November 2026, Sudan's military authorities submitted formal complaints against Ethiopia to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council. They claimed to have provided evidence supporting their allegations. The diplomatic move demonstrated the seriousness of Sudan's concerns and its determination to seek international attention regarding the alleged involvement of its eastern neighbor. Ethiopia, however, has strongly rejected the accusations and made counterclaims against Sudan. Addis Ababa alleges that the Sudanese military is supporting armed rebels operating in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fighting resumed there in September 2026, threatening the peace agreement signed in Pretoria in 2022, which had brought an end to the devastating conflict between Ethiopian federal forces and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Ethiopian military leaders have also accused Sudan, Eritrea, and Egypt of supporting opposition groups seeking to destabilize the country. These allegations have been rejected by the countries concerned. The Ethiopian government maintains that external interference is contributing to its domestic security challenges. The diplomatic confrontation has already produced tangible consequences. In early November, Ethiopia closed the Sudanese consulate in the border town of Asosa and ordered six Sudanese diplomatic staff members to leave the country. Sudan subsequently closed the Ethiopian consulate in Gedaref and expelled its diplomatic personnel. The reciprocal actions marked a further deterioration in relations and reduced opportunities for direct diplomatic communication between the two governments. Several historical and political disputes have contributed to the worsening relationship. One major issue is the disputed Al-Fashaga border region, a fertile agricultural area claimed by both countries. Ethiopian farmers have traditionally cultivated parts of the territory, while Sudan has repeatedly asserted its sovereignty over the region. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved into the disputed area as Ethiopian forces were engaged in fighting in Tigray. The disagreement has remained a significant source of tension. Another important issue is the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), constructed on the Blue Nile River in Ethiopia. Although the dam is expected to strengthen Ethiopia's electricity generation capacity and support economic development, Sudan and Egypt have expressed concerns about its impact on downstream water resources. The absence of a comprehensive, legally binding agreement on the dam's operation and water management has further complicated regional relations. The involvement of external powers has also made the situation more complicated. Different countries have developed competing political and security partnerships across the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia has maintained important relationships with the United Arab Emirates, while Sudan has developed closer ties with Egypt and Eritrea. Turkey has also maintained relations with both countries. These overlapping alliances could make regional diplomacy more difficult if the confrontation intensifies. The humanitarian consequences of the two countries' internal conflicts are already devastating. Sudan's war has killed at least 59,000 people, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, while approximately 13 million people have been displaced. Millions more face food shortages, inadequate medical facilities, and limited access to essential services. Renewed fighting in Ethiopia could create another wave of displacement and place additional pressure on humanitarian organizations. For Bangladesh and other developing countries, instability in the Horn of Africa deserves attention because regional conflicts can disrupt international trade, maritime transportation, energy markets, and global supply chains. The Horn of Africa occupies an important geographical position near the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, through which substantial volumes of international commerce pass. A wider military confrontation could create additional security and economic challenges for countries dependent on international trade. The international community, particularly the United Nations and the African Union, should take urgent diplomatic initiatives to prevent further escalation. Both Ethiopia and Sudan must respect each other's sovereignty and refrain from supporting armed groups operating across international borders. Independent investigations into the allegations could help establish the facts and reduce mutual suspicion. Regular diplomatic communication, confidence-building measures, and peaceful border management are also essential. Ultimately, Ethiopia and Sudan cannot achieve lasting security through mutual accusations and military confrontation. Both countries face serious domestic challenges that require political reconciliation, economic recovery, and humanitarian assistance. Their governments should recognize that regional cooperation is far more beneficial than prolonged hostility. Preventing another major conflict in the Horn of Africa is not only a responsibility of Ethiopia and Sudan but also an important concern for the entire international community. Peaceful dialogue, mutual respect, and adherence to international law remain the best ways to protect regional stability and promote a more secure future. This diplomatic dispute raises concerns about a potential wider conflict in the politically unstable Horn of Africa. Sudan's military has alleged that Ethiopia is harboring the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which are engaged in a civil war against Sudan's Armed Forces, claiming that Ethiopian territory is being used for military operations against Sudan. In response, Ethiopia has accused Sudan of backing rebels in its northern Tigray region, where fighting has resumed, threatening a previous peace agreement. The situation has led to reciprocal closures of consulates and expulsions of diplomatic staff, further straining relations. Historical disputes, particularly over the Al-Fashaga border region and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, complicate matters. The humanitarian impact is severe, with thousands dead and millions displaced, highlighting the urgent need for international diplomatic intervention to prevent further escalation and promote regional stability.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia faces risk of regional war ahead of COP32 climate summit - Ynetnews
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia faces risk of regional war ahead of COP32 climate summit Updates Red Mail 23° Tel Aviv-Jaffa Search Main Israel News Mideast & World News Tech & Digital Real Estate Finance Lifestyle Health & Science Jewish World Travel More Channels Opinions Magazine Sports Food Weather Podcasts Sites & Sources Ynet Calcalist yad2 ynetespanol Вести mynet Contact Contact us Privacy Policy Terms of Use Accessibility Statement Opinion Ethiopia faces risk of regional war ahead of COP32 climate summit Opinion: As Ethiopia prepares to host the COP32 climate summit in 2027, escalating tensions with Eritrea, Sudan and other regional rivals threaten stability in the Horn of Africa, raising concerns over Red Sea security and Israel's strategic interests Amine Ayoub | Add a comment Print Find an error? Report us Related Topics Ethiopia Climate change Addis Ababa From November 8 to 19, 2027, thousands of world leaders, climate negotiators, scientists and financiers will gather in Addis Ababa for 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32). Ethiopia has secured the presidency of the United Nations climate summit, a major diplomatic achievement that places the seat of the African Union at the center of global climate finance and renewable energy talks. Ethiopian officials have presented the event as proof of the country’s emergence as a green powerhouse, citing the Green Legacy reforestation campaign and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Africa’s largest hydroelectric facility. Gallery The security picture has deteriorated quickly. Forces loyal to Ethiopia’s federal government in Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, after recapturing the city from Tigrayan rebels on Oct. 4 ( Photo: Obtained by REUTERS ) Yet the same government is preparing for that spotlight while its neighborhood slides toward confrontation. Ethiopia’s greatest diplomatic success may become a practical constraint on its regional ambitions. Hosting COP32 creates reputational, financial and diplomatic incentives for restraint that Addis Ababa cannot easily ignore. Whether those incentives prove strong enough remains an open question with direct implications for Israel’s security along the Red Sea. The security picture has deteriorated quickly. Tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea escalated after fighting resumed between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan units in September 2026 and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations in response to Addis Ababa's decision to close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats. Troop concentrations near Badme, the flashpoint of the 1998–2000 war, have raised fears of direct confrontation. ACLED reported artillery exchanges and clashes near Badme on November 12 and 13, although Reuters could not independently verify direct fighting between the two armies. The African Union has called for restraint as the risk of wider fighting grows. Ethiopia’s long-standing search for sovereign Red Sea access compounds the problem. The 2024 memorandum with Somaliland triggered sharp opposition from Somalia, which views any arrangement that challenges its territorial integrity as unacceptable. Subsequent diplomacy produced the Ankara Declaration of December 11, 2024. Under that Turkish-facilitated agreement, Ethiopia and Somalia committed to negotiate reliable Ethiopian sea access under Somali sovereignty. The original memorandum created a crisis. The later framework established a different, still fragile path. Progress remains limited and distrust persists on both sides. These disputes have drawn in other regional actors. The October 4 El Alamein Declaration brought Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia together around sovereignty, territorial integrity and regional stability. The text affirms that Red Sea governance belongs to littoral states and rejects unilateral Nile measures that harm downstream countries. It also calls for peaceful solutions and does not name Ethiopia as an adversary. Even so, the declaration functions as a strategic counterweight to Ethiopian influence in both the Nile Basin and the Red Sea corridor. Cairo’s decision to deepen this coordination under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi prioritizes pressure over mediation. Cairo's close coordination with Khartoum, Asmara and Mogadishu increases diplomatic pressure on Addis Ababa. Although the declaration invokes peaceful solutions, its coordination framework strengthens a regional alignment whose positions on Nile waters, Somaliland and Red Sea governance frequently clash with Ethiopian interests. Red Sea ( Photo: Konoplytska/Shutterstock ) The Sisi regime has long treated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a national security issue. Its regional posture amplifies zero-sum competition rather than reducing it. Sudan adds another layer of friction. Khartoum accuses Addis Ababa of supporting the Rapid Support Forces. Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing Tigrayan rebels. Both sides deny the charges. With Sudan already engulfed in civil war, any spillover across the shared border would further destabilize the region and multiply the risks facing civilian populations already suffering from displacement and food shortages. A separate diplomatic rupture between Somalia and the United Arab Emirates has complicated the picture further. Mogadishu expelled the UAE ambassador and earlier canceled agreements on ports, defense and security cooperation. Abu Dhabi rejected the accusations as escalatory. Because Gulf states maintain deep stakes in Red Sea ports and security arrangements, the dispute feeds uncertainty that reaches Addis Ababa’s own calculations. The Somalia-UAE confrontation remains secondary to the core state rivalries, yet it illustrates how quickly bilateral disputes can unsettle an already tense environment. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of these risks. It links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and carries a significant share of global maritime traffic. Any expansion of interstate conflict or further fragmentation of Somalia’s security landscape would create openings for armed groups. Al-Shabaab and residual ISIS-linked networks already operate in the region. They do not require control of capitals to threaten shipping lanes or project violence. Iran-backed Houthi forces have separately demonstrated the ability to disrupt traffic through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb. These threats exist independently. Together they make instability in the Horn a direct concern for Israel. The Red Sea is a strategic corridor for Israel , connecting the region to Asian and East African trade while exposing its southern maritime approaches to hostile forces. Bank of Israel research found that maritime imports from Asia and Oceania amounted to approximately $20 billion in 2023, around one-fifth of Israel's civilian imports. Although shipping diversions following Houthi attacks did not significantly reduce Israeli imports, they demonstrated how instability around Bab el-Mandeb can force vessels onto substantially longer routes and complicate maritime security. A wider crisis in the Horn would expand the operational space available to radical networks whose activities already endanger open sea lanes. Egypt’s contribution under Sisi has been to reinforce competitive alignments rather than to lower temperatures. A foreign policy that prioritizes short-term pressure on Ethiopia is not a stabilizing force. It is a risk multiplier for every state that relies on a secure Red Sea, including Israel. This is the context in which COP32 becomes more than a climate conference. Hosting the summit places Ethiopia under sustained international scrutiny. Foreign ministries, development banks, corporate sponsors and security services will examine the host country’s stability, airspace safety and regional relationships. This scrutiny is already underway. A joint UNFCCC and UN security mission visited Addis Ababa in July 2026 to assess venue, accommodation, transport, security and health preparations. Discussions on the host-country agreement have also begun. Ethiopia cannot afford a full-scale regional war in the months leading to November 2027 without damaging the credibility, attendance and financial success of the event. Major delegations and private investors can revise their plans if northern Ethiopia descends into cross-border fighting or if regional tensions dominate the agenda. Climate vulnerability and political conflict reinforce each other across the Horn. Drought, erratic rainfall, food insecurity and displacement place additional strain on governments already managing internal wars and mutual suspicion. If Addis Ababa intends to present itself as a leader in climate adaptation and cross-border resilience, partners will expect evidence of cooperation closer to home. Ethiopia has already begun framing COP32 as an inclusive platform for dialogue and climate finance delivery. That positioning creates leverage. The summit cannot resolve territorial disputes or replace direct negotiations. It can, however, raise the cost of escalation. Reputational damage, delayed climate financing, postponed investment and diminished international standing are concrete risks. Those risks give Ethiopian decision-makers incentives for restraint that did not exist before the country won the right to host. The prestige of the summit and the economic stakes attached to it may yet encourage cooler calculations in Addis Ababa and among its neighbors in the months ahead. COP32 will not settle the Nile dispute, resolve Ethiopia's maritime ambitions or erase the grievances separating Addis Ababa from its neighbors. But it can make escalation more costly for a government seeking to present itself as a global climate leader. Ethiopia's real test is whether it can translate international prestige into restraint at home and diplomacy abroad. For Israel, the question is whether the states surrounding the Red Sea can contain their rivalries before armed groups and external powers exploit the resulting instability. Amine Ayoub, a fellow at the Middle East Forum, is a policy analyst and writer based in Morocco. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is facing escalating tensions with regional rivals Eritrea and Sudan, raising concerns about potential conflict ahead of the COP32 climate summit scheduled for November 2027 in Addis Ababa. As Ethiopia prepares to host this significant event, which aims to position the country as a leader in climate finance and renewable energy, the deteriorating security situation poses a challenge to its diplomatic ambitions. Recent clashes near the contested Badme region and strained relations with Eritrea have heightened fears of direct confrontation. Additionally, Ethiopia's quest for access to the Red Sea has sparked opposition from Somalia, complicating regional dynamics. The African Union has called for restraint, but the involvement of other nations, including Egypt and Sudan, adds pressure on Ethiopia. The COP32 summit could serve as a platform for dialogue, but it also places Ethiopia under international scrutiny, making it imperative for the government to manage regional tensions to ensure the event's success and maintain its credibility.

His work included community development activities in Beledweyne, central Somalia, and Nairobi, Kenya. ON Omar Nor, Chief Editor · GAROWE ONLINE 23 Nov 2026 · 11:26 · 1 min read MOGADISHU – Ali Abdullahi Cosoble, the first president of Somalia’s Hirshabelle state, has died in Egypt at the age of 65, marking the passing of a politician who played a key role in the establishment of the regional administration. Cosoble died on Sunday night at a hospital in Egypt, where he had been receiving medical treatment in recent days following an illness, according to family members and Somali politicians. Hirshabelle President Ali Gudlawe Hussein and other officials expressed condolences following news of his death, praying for Allah to grant him mercy and give his family and the Somali people strength during their loss. Born in Mogadishu on June 15, 1961, Cosoble received his higher education in the United States, graduating from Sam Houston State University. Before entering politics, he worked with several institutions, including the Somali Development Bank and international aid organisation Oxfam. His work included community development activities in Beledweyne, central Somalia, and Nairobi, Kenya. Cosoble later became involved in national politics, serving as a member of Somalia’s Transitional Federal Parliament from 2004 to 2012. In 2005, he was appointed federal minister of education, adding to his experience in public service. His most prominent political role came in 2016, when he became the first president of Hirshabelle, a federal member state formed through the merger of Hiiraan and Middle Shabelle regions. He was elected on October 17, 2016, during efforts to establish federal administrations across Somalia as part of the country's federalisation process. His presidency, however, was marked by political disagreements. In August 2017, Hirshabelle's regional parliament voted to remove him from office following a political dispute, bringing his tenure to an end less than a year after his election. Despite his departure from office, Cosoble remained part of Somalia's political landscape and was remembered for his role in the formation of Hirshabelle and its early administration. His death has prompted condolences from political leaders and officials, highlighting his contribution to Somalia's federal political development. somalia.summary: Ali Abdullahi Cosoble, the first president of Somalia's Hirshabelle state, passed away in Egypt at the age of 65 after a recent illness. His death was confirmed by family members and Somali politicians, prompting condolences from current Hirshabelle President Ali Gudlawe Hussein and others. Born in Mogadishu on June 15, 1961, Cosoble pursued higher education in the United States, graduating from Sam Houston State University. Before his political career, he worked with the Somali Development Bank and Oxfam, focusing on community development in Beledweyne and Nairobi. Cosoble served in Somalia’s Transitional Federal Parliament from 2004 to 2012 and was appointed federal minister of education in 2005. He became Hirshabelle's first president in 2016, a role marked by political challenges that led to his removal in 2017. Despite his short tenure, he is remembered for his contributions to Somalia's federal political landscape and the establishment of Hirshabelle.

somalia.title: Six Somali Supreme Court judges sue federal government at East African Court of Justice - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Six Somali Supreme Court judges sue federal government at East African Court of Justice - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Six Somali Supreme Court judges sue federal government at East African Court of Justice Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Six Somali Supreme Court judges, including disputed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed, have filed a case against the federal government at the East African Court of Justice (EACJ). In a formal notice dated Nov. 18, the court's First Instance Division in Arusha, Tanzania, gave Somalia's attorney general 45 days from the date of service to respond to the case, registered as Reference No. 69 of 2026. advertisements The notice warned that if the government fails to submit a response within the specified period, the court may proceed to hear and determine the case in its absence. “You are hereby required to file a response within 45 days from the day of service hereof. In default whereof, the reference will be heard and determined in your absence,” the court's notice said. The six applicants are Baashe Yusuf Ahmed, Salah Sheikh Ibrahim Diblawe, Abdulkadir Idris Essa, Abubakar Ahmed Ali, Abdikafar Hussein Isak and Abdiaziz Mohamed Yusuf. The lawsuit names the State Attorney General and the Federal Republic of Somalia as respondents. The judges are challenging actions taken by the federal government following President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's Nov. 4 decision to dismiss Baashe from his position as chief justice. They are also seeking judicial examination of alleged interference with the Supreme Court's independence and the disruption of its operations following the dispute between the presidency and the judiciary. The legal action follows a confrontation that began when Hassan Sheikh removed Baashe a day before the Supreme Court was scheduled to rule on the constitutionality of amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years. On Nov. 5, a five-judge panel ruled that the constitutional amendments could not be applied retroactively to current officeholders. The court declared that Hassan Sheikh's presidential mandate expired May 15, 2026, while the mandates of both houses of the federal parliament ended April 14. It directed political stakeholders to reach an agreement on an electoral framework within 30 days and ordered elections to be held within 90 days. The Supreme Court also declared Baashe's dismissal unconstitutional, arguing that the president lacked the authority to remove the chief justice unilaterally without following the required constitutional procedures. The federal government rejected the rulings, maintaining that the constitutional amendments provide a legal basis for the current administration to remain in office until elections scheduled for 2027. Somalia's attorney general also challenged the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and questioned the legal standing of the proceedings. Despite the court's objections, Hassan Sheikh presided over the swearing-in of Ibrahim Idle Suleiman as chief justice on Nov. 7, further intensifying the dispute over the leadership of the country's highest judicial institution. The controversy has also drawn international criticism. On Nov. 12, United Nations human rights experts condemned Baashe's dismissal, describing it as interference with judicial independence. The experts alleged that several Supreme Court judges had been deprived of their security protection and subjected to restrictions on their movements. They called for Baashe's reinstatement, the restoration of security arrangements for judges and an end to actions they said were undermining the independence of the judiciary. The latest lawsuit moves the dispute into the East African Community's regional judicial system, where the six judges are seeking legal review of the federal government's actions. Somalia became a full member of the East African Community in 2024, bringing it within the regional framework that includes the East African Court of Justice. The EACJ is responsible for interpreting and applying the East African Community Treaty and considering disputes falling within its jurisdiction. The Nov. 18 notice marks the beginning of the formal response process and does not constitute a ruling on the legality of Baashe's dismissal or the Supreme Court's disputed constitutional decisions. The federal government has not publicly announced how it intends to respond to the regional court proceedings. The case adds another legal dimension to Somalia's political crisis as disagreements continue over constitutional reforms, presidential and parliamentary mandates, and the timetable for national elections. The judges are contesting the alleged interference with the Supreme Court's independence and operations, particularly after a ruling on constitutional amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms. somalia.title: Somalia, Algeria's Sonatrach Strengthen Energy Cooperation Amid Growing Interest in Oil and Gas Sector - Horseed Media
somalia.content: Somalia, Algeria's Sonatrach Strengthen Energy Cooperation Amid Growing Interest in Oil and Gas Sector | Horseed Media Skip to content Search Home Somalia News Puntland News World News in English Featured More.. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia, Algeria’s Sonatrach Strengthen Energy Cooperation Amid Growing Interest in Oil and Gas Sector Posted by: Horseed Staff MOGADISHU – Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on Sunday received a delegation from Algeria’s state-owned oil and gas company, Sonatrach, at the presidential palace, as the two sides seek to strengthen cooperation in oil exploration, gas development and natural resource management. 22 November, 2026 Share Tweet The delegation was led by Mohamed Ghrab, Director of Laboratories at Sonatrach’s Exploration and Production Directorate, according to the Somali National News Agency. The meeting followed a series of engagements between Sonatrach representatives and Somali petroleum officials in Mogadishu over the past week. These included a visit to the national oil depot at the Port of Mogadishu and technical discussions with the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources. The discussions reflect growing efforts by Somalia to develop its emerging hydrocarbons sector through international partnerships, technical expertise and institutional capacity building. Partnership Focuses on Technical Expertise and Training Sonatrach’s engagement with Somalia is part of a broader strategic partnership established during President Mohamud’s visit to Algeria in 2025, when the two countries signed an agreement covering cooperation in oil, gas and mineral resources. Since then, the partnership has focused primarily on knowledge transfer, professional training and strengthening Somalia’s technical capacity rather than direct commercial investment. During discussions at the Port of Mogadishu on November 16, Sonatrach representatives expressed their readiness to share expertise in oil exploration, production and refining, while also supporting the training of Somali petroleum engineers. Somalia’s Deputy Minister of Petroleum, Abdiwahab Abdi Omar Ananug, welcomed the proposed cooperation, stressing the importance of developing domestic expertise to enable the country to manage and exploit its natural resources independently. He said Somalia needed partners willing to help the country develop its own production capabilities rather than simply supply finished petroleum products. The partnership also includes an Algerian commitment to provide 500 scholarships to Somali students, including opportunities in petroleum engineering. The scholarships were announced during President Mohamud’s 2025 visit to Algeria. The Somali Petroleum Authority has indicated that further announcements regarding the initiative are expected, although specific details have yet to be made public. No Exploration or Investment Agreement Announced Despite the high-level engagement at Villa Somalia, neither government has announced an agreement authorising Sonatrach to undertake oil exploration or make direct investments in Somalia’s petroleum sector. For now, the company’s publicly outlined commitments centre on technical assistance, professional training and the transfer of expertise. Somali authorities have also not disclosed a timetable indicating when Sonatrach could move beyond advisory and capacity-building support towards operational activities in the country. The distinction is significant as Somalia seeks to attract international energy companies while building the regulatory, technical and institutional capacity needed to manage its natural resources. Algeria Emerges as a Strategic Partner Sonatrach, widely recognised as Africa’s largest oil and gas company, brings extensive experience in hydrocarbon exploration, production, processing and refining. Its growing engagement with Somalia could provide an important opportunity for the country to benefit from Algeria’s decades of experience in developing and managing a major petroleum industry. Beyond the energy sector, the partnership also carries broader diplomatic significance. Algeria has consistently supported Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and has publicly opposed Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, placing the two countries on common ground over Somalia’s territorial unity. For Mogadishu, closer cooperation with Algiers offers an opportunity to strengthen both economic and diplomatic relations while seeking international expertise to develop its natural resource sector. Although the latest discussions have not produced a publicly announced exploration or investment deal, the engagement signals continued momentum in Somalia’s efforts to establish partnerships that could support the long-term development of its oil and gas industry. The partnership, established during President Mohamud's 2025 visit to Algeria, focuses on knowledge transfer, professional training, and building Somalia's technical capacity rather than direct commercial investment. somalia.title: Somalia Says Army Is Ready to Take Over as Uganda Begins Troop Withdrawal - Horseed Media
somalia.content: Somalia Says Army Is Ready to Take Over as Uganda Begins Troop Withdrawal | Horseed Media Skip to content Search Home Somalia News Puntland News World News in English Featured More.. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia Says Army Is Ready to Take Over as Uganda Begins Troop Withdrawal Posted by: Horseed Staff MOGADISHU – Somalia’s government says its armed forces are prepared to assume responsibility for security positions currently held by Ugandan troops, as Kampala gradually withdraws its forces from the country after nearly two decades of supporting efforts to combat the Al-Shabaab insurgency. 22 November, 2026 Share Tweet The transition gathered momentum on 15 November when Ugandan troops serving under the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) handed over five military bases in and around Barawe, a strategic port town in the Lower Shabelle region, to the Somali National Army (SNA). The facilities, which include positions at the seaport and airstrip, were fully operational at the time of the handover, according to Uganda’s military. Somalia’s Information Minister, Abdifatah Qasim Mahmoud, expressed confidence in the country’s ability to maintain security following the departure of foreign troops. “We are not concerned that this will change the security situation in the country or in the areas these troops are leaving,” Mahmoud said during a BBC Somali debate on Friday. However, the government’s confidence has been challenged by concerns over the readiness of Somali forces to independently secure areas previously protected by African Union peacekeepers. During the same programme, lawmaker Ahmed Abdi Kooshin argued that Somalia was not yet prepared to assume full responsibility for the positions. He pointed to Mogadishu and parts of the Lower and Middle Shabelle regions, which he said continued to depend on AU forces for security. He also warned that Al-Shabaab had managed to retake some territories. Mahmoud defended the government’s position, citing military operations between Mogadishu and Harardhere in which Somali forces had led efforts to reclaim territory from the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group. He said the government had spent five years strengthening and training the national army, adding that some soldiers had recently returned from training programmes abroad. The minister also described the direct transfer of military bases as evidence of growing confidence in the capabilities of Somali forces. He stressed that foreign troops had been deployed for a limited period and that Somalia ultimately needed to rely on its own security institutions while maintaining cooperation with international partners. The United Nations secretary-general said in October that joint military operations had improved security in Mogadishu, although Al-Shabaab remained the principal security threat across southern and central Somalia. In July, coordinated attacks by the militant group against three African Union bases in Lower Shabelle were repelled, according to a UN report. Uganda’s Withdrawal to Continue Through 2027 Uganda’s military announced on 2 November that it had begun returning some troops serving under a separate bilateral security agreement with Mogadishu. It also confirmed that the withdrawal of its contingent from the African Union mission would take place in phases, with all Ugandan troops expected to leave Somalia by the end of 2027. Uganda was the first country to deploy troops to the original African Union mission in Somalia in 2007. At the beginning of the current withdrawal process, approximately 4,500 Ugandan soldiers were serving under AUSSOM. The strategic town of Barawe was captured from Al-Shabaab by Somali and African Union forces in 2014 and has remained an important location in the country’s security architecture. As part of the wider transition, the African Union has developed plans to relocate peacekeepers from Barawe to four military bases near Mogadishu to replace troops departing under Uganda’s separate bilateral deployment. In a letter dated 31 October to the United Nations support office, the AU described the four positions as critical to the defence of the Somali capital, according to a document obtained by The Associated Press . Meanwhile, Uganda’s military said on Sunday that its land forces commander, Lieutenant General Kayanja Muhanga, had visited Ugandan troops still serving under AUSSOM. During the visit, he reviewed the withdrawal process in Barawe and assessed the operational readiness of the remaining forces. Somalia and AU Review Security Transition Plans Somalia and the African Union have also intensified discussions on the next stages of the security handover. Officials from both sides opened talks in Mogadishu on Wednesday to coordinate the transition and ensure that the withdrawal of foreign troops does not leave security gaps that could be exploited by Al-Shabaab. AUSSOM Force Commander Lieutenant General Sam Kavuma said the priority was to ensure a smooth transfer of responsibilities without compromising the security gains achieved over the years. “Our priority is to ensure that the gradual transfer of security responsibilities does not create operational gaps or undermine the gains achieved,” Kavuma said. The Somali government also presented its proposed transition arrangements to international partners during separate discussions in Brussels on Thursday. Opening the meeting, Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi outlined the security situation on the ground and the government’s preparations for assuming greater responsibility for national security. According to Somalia’s Defence Ministry, Fiqi called on international partners to support a transition process guided by the country’s priorities and security requirements. The discussions come ahead of an important United Nations Security Council decision next month on whether to renew AUSSOM’s mandate, which is scheduled to expire on 31 December. The European Union said the Brussels meeting had contributed to preparations for the upcoming Security Council deliberations. A US State Department spokesperson told Agence France-Presse on 15 November that Washington would support a one-year extension of AUSSOM’s mandate and that of the United Nations office providing logistical support to the mission. Wider International Withdrawal Timeline Despite Uganda’s decision to withdraw its forces by the end of 2027, the African Union’s broader security transition plan envisages a gradual withdrawal of international peacekeepers by December 2029. The pace of the process will depend largely on security conditions and the ability of Somali forces to assume responsibility for protecting key towns, military installations and strategic infrastructure. The transition represents a significant test for Somalia’s security institutions, which have spent years building their capacity to confront Al-Shabaab. While the government maintains that its forces are increasingly capable of leading national security operations, concerns remain over the sustainability of military gains and the possibility that militant fighters could exploit gaps created by the departure of foreign troops. The coming months are therefore likely to be crucial in determining whether Somalia can successfully take greater control of its security while preserving the progress achieved through nearly two decades of international military support. somalia.summary: Somalia's government has announced that its armed forces are ready to take over security responsibilities as Uganda begins withdrawing its troops after nearly two decades of support against the Al-Shabaab insurgency. The transition gained momentum on November 15 when Ugandan troops handed over five military bases in the Lower Shabelle region to the Somali National Army (SNA). Somalia's Information Minister, Abdifatah Qasim Mahmoud, expressed confidence in the SNA's ability to maintain security, despite concerns from some lawmakers about the readiness of Somali forces to fill the security gaps left by departing African Union peacekeepers. Uganda's military plans to withdraw all its troops by the end of 2027, with the African Union also coordinating a broader transition of peacekeepers by December 2029. The success of this transition is critical for Somalia's security, as it seeks to confront Al-Shabaab independently while ensuring that recent military gains are not compromised.

(2026) Asaf Türk 23 Nov 2026 09:07 Updated: 11 Nov 2026 0 Show Article Summary Somalia’s Military Power: How Many Tanks, Aircraft and Ships Are in the Inventory? (2026) Summary Not Found. Bottom line: Somalia ranks 137th of 145 countries in Global Firepower 2026 (PwrIndx 3.7393). GFP counts 30,000 active and 2,000 paramilitary personnel, 1,104 vehicles, 6 helicopters and 19 patrol craft; the tank, artillery and fighter entries are zero. The army, which dissolved in 1991, has been rebuilt since 2008, and Türkiye is the largest partner in that process: the TURKSOM training base, Gorgor special forces, BMC Kirpi, T129 ATAK, Bayraktar TB2 and Akıncı, and the 2024 Defence and Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement. Somalia’s military inventory tells the story of an armed force that once had one of Africa’s largest armies, dissolved together with the state in 1991 and was then rebuilt almost from scratch. Equipped with Soviet tanks and MiG aircraft under Siad Barre, the army today fights al-Shabaab with mine-resistant vehicles, light infantry, drones and a small number of helicopters. In this rebuilding Türkiye is the broadest partner, from training to the navy. This article reads Global Firepower, IISS, SIPRI and open-source data together, and states from the outset that the figures are approximate and that some deliveries have not been officially confirmed. Table of Contents At a Glance About the Somalia Armed Forces Land Forces Inventory Air Force Inventory Missile and Air-Defence Systems Naval Power The Turkey Angle: Turkish Defence Industry Frequently Asked Questions Bottom Line Related Reading Sources At a Glance Active personnel: Global Firepower counts 30,000 active and 2,000 paramilitary personnel with no reserves; the army has been rebuilt from scratch since 2008 after the collapse of the state in 1991 Main battle tanks: GFP shows zero; open-source reports said M48 and M60 tanks were unloaded at Mogadishu port in February 2026, but numbers and status have not been officially announced Armoured vehicles: GFP counts 1,104 vehicles; the core consists of mine-resistant vehicles such as the Turkish-made BMC Kirpi, the South African Casspir, Mamba and Puma, and the British Saxon Artillery and rocket launchers: GFP gives zero for self-propelled guns, towed guns and rocket launchers; the army works mainly with light infantry and mortars Military aircraft: GFP counts 6 helicopters; according to open sources 3 T129 ATAKs delivered in June 2025 were added, and Bayraktar TB2 and Akıncı drones are also in the inventory Defence budget: GFP shows 870 million dollars; a large part of the army’s pay, training and equipment burden is covered with support from partners such as Türkiye, the US, the UAE, Qatar and the European Union Note: The inventory figures below are approximate values drawn from open sources such as Global Firepower, the IISS Military Balance and SIPRI. About the Somalia Armed Forces The Somali Armed Forces consist of the Somali National Army, the Air Force and the Navy. The army’s prominent units are the US-backed Danab and the Türkiye-trained Gorgor (Eagle) brigades. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term was extended by a constitutional amendment in March 2026, a decision contested by the opposition; the electoral commission has scheduled the presidential election for 15 May 2027. The African Union mission AUSSOM, which replaced ATMIS in January 2025, still plays an important security role with about 11,000 troops. In the Global Firepower 2026 ranking Somalia is 137th of 145 with a PwrIndx of 3.7393. GFP takes the population as about 13 million and lists 30,000 active and 2,000 paramilitary personnel, with no reserves. The defence budget is 870 million dollars in GFP. A large part of the army’s pay, training and equipment burden is covered with support from partners such as Türkiye, the US, the UAE, Qatar and the European Union, so the budget figure alone may not reflect real spending. The land inventory rests on light and protected mobility. GFP counts 1,104 vehicles, and the entries for tanks, self-propelled guns, towed guns and rocket launchers are zero. The core consists of the Turkish-made BMC Kirpi and Kirpi II, the South African Casspir, Mamba and Puma, the British Saxon, the French ACMAT Bastion and UAE-made Streit vehicles. Open-source reports said M48 and M60 tanks were carried to Mogadishu aboard TCG Sancaktar in February 2026; because numbers and status have not been officially announced, this article does not treat them as a firm inventory figure. Air power rests not on fixed-wing aircraft but on helicopters and drones. GFP counts 6 helicopters. According to open sources, 3 T129 ATAK attack helicopters and 2 utility helicopters for the Navy were delivered in June 2025; the T129s flew over Mogadishu in the 1 July 2025 Independence Day parade. Wikipedia also notes that Turkish officials reportedly said these helicopters remained under Turkish control. The Bayraktar TB2 has been used against al-Shabaab since 2022, and at least 2 Bayraktar Akıncı reached the country in March 2025. Somalia has no surface-to-air missile system or ballistic missiles; the SA-2 and SA-3 systems of the 1980s were lost with the collapse of the state. Light anti-aircraft guns are mostly mounted on pickups for ground support. Deterrence in the airspace relies largely on partners: Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence released footage of F-16s flying over Mogadishu at the 12 April 2026 parade for the 66th anniversary of the Somali Armed Forces, officially showing Turkish combat aircraft deployed in Somalia for the first time. According to GFP, the Navy tries to protect 3,025 km of coastline, the longest of mainland Africa, with 19 patrol craft; there are no frigates, corvettes or submarines. The Wikipedia list also includes Turkish-made ONUK MRTP 16 patrol boats. The rebuilding of the Navy was tied to Türkiye by the 10-year Defence and Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement signed in Ankara on 8 February 2024. The main tasks are countering piracy, illegal fishing and arms smuggling in the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Land Forces Inventory System type Est. quantity Main battle tanks GFP says zero. Source: Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Air Force Inventory Platform Est. quantity Total military aircraft GFP counts 6 aircraft, all helicopters; there are no fixed-wing fighters, transports or trainers. The Somali Air Force effectively dissolved after 1991 and is being re-established Attack and utility helicopters 3 T129 ATAKs were delivered in June 2025 and flew in the 1 July 2025 parade; Wikipedia also notes that Turkish officials reportedly said the helicopters remained under Turkish control. On the utility side there are Bell 205/412-class helicopters and 2 helicopters handed to the Navy Unmanned aerial vehicles The Bayraktar TB2 has been used in operations against al-Shabaab since 2022; at least 2 Bayraktar Akıncı arrived in Somalia in March 2025. These systems are the backbone of the country’s real air power Missile and Air-Defence Systems System Type / Note Ballistic and cruise missiles None. There are no ballistic or cruise missiles in the Somali inventory Air-defence missiles There is no surface-to-air missile system. Soviet SA-2 and SA-3 systems existed in the 1980s and were lost entirely with the collapse of the state Anti-aircraft guns Light systems such as the ZU-23-2 and DShK are used mostly mounted on pickups for ground support External air cover Deterrence in Somali airspace relies largely on partners. In April 2026 Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence for the first time officially showed Turkish F-16s deployed in Somalia An Agusta-Bell 412 helicopter used for Somali Air Force pilot training, at the 1 July 2025 Independence Day parade. Somalia has no surface-to-air missile system; deterrence in its airspace relies on partners. Photo: Mohamed A. Muhumed, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Naval Power Class / Type Est. quantity Patrol craft GFP counts 19 patrol craft; there are no frigates, corvettes or submarines. The Wikipedia list includes Turkish-made ONUK MRTP 16 patrol boats and rigid inflatable boats Rebuilding framework The 10-year Defence and Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement signed in Ankara on 8 February 2024 tied the rebuilding, training and equipping of the Somali Navy to Türkiye; the Somali parliament approved it in February 2024 Coastline and mission According to GFP, 3,025 km of coastline, the longest of mainland Africa; the main mission is countering piracy, illegal fishing and arms smuggling in the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean Somali naval cadets graduating at TURKSOM, congratulated by a Turkish officer (2018). Source: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.5). The Turkey Angle: Turkish Defence Industry Somalia has one of Türkiye’s most comprehensive defence partnerships in Africa. At its centre is TURKSOM (Turkish Task Force Command in Somalia), opened in Mogadishu on 30 September 2017: Türkiye’s largest overseas military training facility, it has trained thousands of Somali soldiers to date and has capacity to train more than 10,000. The Türkiye-trained Gorgor (Eagle) brigades and Haramcad police special operations units are among the leading elements of operations against al-Shabaab. On the equipment side, Turkish platforms form the most modern layer of the inventory. The first batch of BMC Kirpi was delivered to Gorgor units in 2021, followed by the Kirpi II; the infantry uses the Turkish-made MPT-76 rifle and MG3 machine gun. The Bayraktar TB2 has been in Somalia since 2022 and the Bayraktar Akıncı since March 2025. In June 2025, after about a year of pilot training, 3 T129 ATAKs and 2 utility helicopters for the Navy were delivered; the helicopters were reported to have been used against al-Shabaab. The institutional framework widened with the 10-year Defence and Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement signed in Ankara on 8 February 2024: Türkiye took on a joint role in rebuilding the Somali Navy and protecting the coastline. This was followed by a hydrocarbon cooperation agreement in March 2024 and the seismic survey mission of Oruç Reis in autumn 2024. Türkiye also hosted the Ankara Declaration of 11 December 2024, which eased tensions between Somalia and Ethiopia. The number of Turkish troops in the country was put at about 500 in mid-2025. In 2026 the partnership extended to air and land components. Turkish F-16s were seen in Mogadishu from January 2026, and the Ministry of National Defence confirmed the deployment with footage in April 2026. Open-source reports said M48 and M60 tanks were carried to Mogadishu aboard TCG Sancaktar in February 2026; the number and whether the tanks are assigned to the Somali army or to protecting Turkish facilities have not been officially announced. Patrol vessels for the navy, coastal surveillance, additional drones and armoured vehicles stand out as natural growth areas for Turkish industry in the period ahead. Frequently Asked Questions How many tanks does Somalia have? Global Firepower shows zero. Open-source reports said M48 and M60 tanks were carried to Mogadishu in February 2026, but numbers and status have not been officially announced. Does Somalia have fighter jets? No. According to GFP all 6 aircraft are helicopters. Somalia’s real air power rests on T129 ATAK helicopters and Bayraktar TB2 and Akıncı drones; the F-16s deployed in Somalia belong to Türkiye. What has Somalia bought from Türkiye? According to open sources: BMC Kirpi and Kirpi II armoured vehicles, MPT-76 rifles, Bayraktar TB2 and Akıncı drones, 3 T129 ATAKs and 2 helicopters for the Navy. Thousands of soldiers have also been trained by Türkiye at TURKSOM. What is TURKSOM? The Turkish Task Force Command in Somalia, opened in Mogadishu on 30 September 2017 and Türkiye’s largest overseas military training base. The Gorgor brigades are trained there. How many ships does the Somali Navy have? GFP counts 19 patrol craft; there are no frigates, corvettes or submarines. The rebuilding of the Navy is carried out under the Türkiye-Somalia Defence and Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement of 8 February 2024. Bottom Line The Somali inventory looks small in numbers: zero tanks, artillery and fighters, 1,104 vehicles, 6 helicopters and 19 patrol craft. But the picture shows an army that dissolved in 1991 being rebuilt while fighting al-Shabaab, and Türkiye is the deepest partner in that process. TURKSOM, the Gorgor brigades, the BMC Kirpi, the Bayraktar TB2 and Akıncı, the T129 ATAK and the 2024 navy agreement make Somalia one of the most comprehensive fields of application for the Turkish defence industry in Africa. The political transition and the 2027 elections will shape the security environment, while needs for the navy, coastal surveillance and armoured vehicles will keep growing in the coming years. somalia.summary: As of 2026, Somalia's military capabilities are limited, ranking 137th out of 145 countries in the Global Firepower index. The armed forces consist of approximately 30,000 active personnel and 2,000 paramilitary members, with no reserves. The inventory includes 1,104 vehicles, primarily mine-resistant types, but lacks main battle tanks, artillery, and fixed-wing aircraft. The air force comprises six helicopters, including three T129 ATAK attack helicopters and drones like the Bayraktar TB2, which have been utilized against al-Shabaab. The navy operates 19 patrol craft, focusing on countering piracy and illegal fishing along its extensive coastline. Turkey plays a significant role in rebuilding Somalia's military, providing training and equipment through agreements established since 2008. The Somali military's modernization efforts are ongoing, with support from various international partners, including the U.S. and the EU, amidst a backdrop of political challenges and security concerns.

The ocean crossing highlights the species' endurance and transcontinental migration route. Advertisement During their migration, Amur Falcons travel through India, with the northeastern states serving as important stopover regions. By: India Today Science Desk New Delhi , Nov 23, 2026 11:12 IST Last Updated Nov 23, 2026 11:12 IST Published by Sibu Kumar Tripathi Nov 23, 2026 11:12 IST In an extraordinary display of endurance, a tiny Amur Falcon named Apapang has completed a breathtaking 5,400-kilometre non-stop flight from Manipur in India to the shores of Somalia in Africa, highlighting one of the most remarkable journeys undertaken by migratory birds. The male Amur Falcon took off from Tamenglong in Manipur and crossed thousands of kilometres over the Indian Ocean before reaching Somalia without making a single stop. The remarkable development was shared by IAS Supriya Sahu, who described the bird's arrival as a miracle of nature. advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story With Apapang now reaching Somalia, another young female Amur Falcon named Alang, which had arrived earlier, has also completed this challenging leg of the transcontinental migration. "Apapang too has done it, arriving in Somalia after 5,400 kms NONSTOP flying," Sahu, Additional Chief Secretary, EDII, Goverment of Tamil Nadu said, celebrating the arrival of the two birds on the African coast. The journey from the hills of Manipur to the Horn of Africa is part of the Amur Falcon's extraordinary annual migration. These small raptors undertake one of the longest migratory journeys among birds of prey, travelling between their breeding grounds in northeastern Asia and wintering grounds in southern Africa. During their migration, Amur Falcons travel through India , with the northeastern states serving as important stopover regions. Nagaland and Manipur, in particular, have become crucial locations for these birds as they prepare for their demanding journey across the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean. The non-stop ocean crossing is particularly remarkable because the birds must sustain flight for extended periods without access to food, water or resting grounds. Their ability to navigate vast stretches of open ocean makes them among nature's most impressive long-distance travellers. The arrival of Apapang and Alang in Somalia marks another milestone in their migration, offering a glimpse into the extraordinary navigational abilities and physical endurance of these tiny birds. From Manipur's forested hills to the African coastline, their journey is shows how wildlife connects continents through natural migration routes that span thousands of kilometres. - Ends Advertisement Also Watch PM questions corporate India over salaries; Trump, Putin, Xi sign peace declaration Tamil Nadu govt removes 15 officials over alleged data leak to Andhra US, Russia, China unveil Shenzhen Declaration; is new tripolar world order emerging? This extraordinary journey showcases the bird's incredible migratory capabilities, as it crossed the Indian Ocean without any stops for food or rest. somalia.title: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Bitcoin briefly fell below $56,000 on Saturday, Nov. 21, hitting its lowest level in more than two years as a stronger U.S. dollar and uncertainty over American interest rates weighed on cryptocurrency markets. The world's largest cryptocurrency dropped to approximately $55,000 before recovering toward $60,000 later in the day. The decline left Bitcoin more than 50% below its October 2025 peak of over $126,000. advertisements For most Somali households, however, the cryptocurrency selloff has little direct effect on everyday spending. Commerce in Mogadishu, Hargeisa and other major cities relies heavily on U.S. dollars transferred through mobile money services rather than Bitcoin. The more immediate concern is the strengthening U.S. dollar, which can increase the cost of sending remittances for Somali workers earning their incomes in other currencies. Bitcoin's latest decline comes amid growing uncertainty in international financial markets over U.S. interest rates, inflation and the outlook for economic growth. Investors have reassessed expectations for Federal Reserve monetary policy, contributing to a stronger dollar and increasing pressure on risk-sensitive assets, including cryptocurrencies and technology stocks. The U.S. Dollar Index, which measures the dollar against a basket of major currencies, approached 104 during the week, reportedly its highest level in approximately 19 months. A stronger dollar can make dollar-denominated investments more expensive for international investors, while expectations of higher interest rates can increase the attractiveness of cash and government bonds relative to speculative assets. Bitcoin has also faced selling pressure from institutional investors, including funds holding the cryptocurrency through exchange-traded products. Institutional selling, combined with the forced liquidation of leveraged trading positions, has contributed to sharp price movements. The latest selloff highlights Bitcoin's continued vulnerability to changes in global financial conditions, despite its frequent promotion as a digital alternative to traditional stores of value. Somalia is among the economies most dependent on remittances from citizens living and working abroad. According to the Central Bank of Somalia's 2025 annual report, individual remittances reached $3.13 billion, up from $2.72 billion in 2024. These transfers represented approximately 24% of Somalia's gross domestic product in 2025, demonstrating their importance to household consumption and economic stability. Remittances help families pay for food, housing, education, healthcare and other basic necessities. Unlike countries where households primarily use domestic currencies, Somalia's economy is heavily dollarized. Many consumers receive, store and spend U.S. dollars through mobile money platforms such as EVC Plus, Zaad and Sahal. This system means changes in the dollar's international value can directly affect the cost of remittances for Somali workers living abroad. For example, a Somali worker in London earning British pounds must convert those earnings into U.S. dollars before sending money home. If the pound falls from $1.35 to $1.31, sending $200 would cost approximately £153 instead of £148, excluding transfer fees. The difference may appear modest for a single transaction, but repeated monthly transfers can become more expensive for workers supporting relatives in Somalia. The same pressure affects Somali workers earning euros, Canadian dollars and other currencies that weaken against the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar does not necessarily reduce the amount received by a family in Somalia if the sender continues transferring the same dollar amount. Instead, it increases the cost for senders earning weaker foreign currencies. Somalia's reliance on the U.S. dollar provides some protection against exchange-rate instability compared with economies that depend on rapidly depreciating domestic currencies. However, dollarization does not shield households from inflation or increases in international commodity prices. Somalia imports substantial quantities of food, fuel, construction materials and manufactured goods, making domestic prices sensitive to changes in global supply chains, transportation costs and commodity markets. Rising energy prices, shipping disruptions and supply shortages can increase the cost of imported products, even when transactions are conducted in dollars. A stronger dollar can also reduce the dollar cost of goods priced in weaker foreign currencies, meaning its effect on Somalia's import bill depends on the product, supplier and market conditions. According to the International Monetary Fund's October 2026 assessment, Somalia's inflation rate is projected to reach 6.5% in 2026. Higher living costs, combined with pressure on remittance senders abroad, could place additional financial strain on households already facing economic and humanitarian challenges. Families that depend on regular financial assistance from relatives overseas may be particularly vulnerable if senders reduce the frequency or value of transfers because of unfavorable exchange rates. Although Bitcoin remains a speculative investment for many traders, dollar-pegged stablecoins such as USDT serve a different purpose. Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a value linked to an underlying asset, usually the U.S. dollar. Some Somali freelancers and cross-border traders use stablecoins to transfer funds internationally without relying entirely on traditional banking channels. However, stablecoins carry their own risks, including issuer, liquidity, regulatory and technical risks, and their dollar pegs are not guaranteed. For most Somali households, conventional remittance companies and mobile money services remain more relevant than cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin's decline illustrates how global financial markets react to changing expectations about interest rates, inflation and the strength of the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar can increase the international purchasing power of dollar holdings, but it can also make dollar-denominated remittances more expensive for relatives earning income in other currencies. somalia.title: Somalia must reject Ethiopia’s “necklace of ports” - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia must reject Ethiopia’s “necklace of ports” - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia must reject Ethiopia’s “necklace of ports” Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hussein Soyan Sunday November 22, 2026 Ethiopia’s need for the sea is legitimate, but Somalia’s coastline is not for sale. Proposals for permanent, sovereign zones on Somali soil should be refused, and Somalis must end their divisions before others exploit them. Ethiopia’s case for reliable access to the sea is a serious one. It is a landlocked country of more than 120 million people, and almost all of its trade passes through the ports of its neighbours. Somalia should acknowledge this. Somali ports could serve Ethiopian commerce on fair terms, and both nations would benefit from such an arrangement. The question is not whether Ethiopia should have access to the sea, but on what terms, and on whose land. That question became sharper this month. On 4 November, in a Middle East Eye podcastwith David Hearst, Alexander Rondos, the former EU special representative for the Horn of Africa, set out his view of Ethiopia’s options. He said Ethiopia should seek access “in perpetuity”, including sovereign access: a port area of one or two square kilometres guarded by Ethiopian troops. Ethiopia, he argued, should aim for “a guaranteed necklace of ports” around it; without one, it feels it has “a noose” around its neck. His advice to Addis Ababa was not to settle for the noose but to find the necklace, and he said he had told Ethiopian leaders as much himself. advertisements Somalis should be clear about what this means. A necklace of ports around Ethiopia can only be made from the coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia and Kenya. Each port on it would be a piece of another country placed under Ethiopian sovereignty, guarded by Ethiopian soldiers, with no end date. That is not a trade agreement. It is a transfer of territory, described in the language of diplomacy. Describing dependence on neighbouring ports as a “noose” casts those neighbours as a threat to be escaped rather than partners to be dealt with fairly. Somalia should reject the idea in full. The reason Rondos gave for a sovereign zone is itself revealing. Ethiopia, he said, would need such an area so that it could import “sensitive material” without it being inspected by anyone else. A zone where Somali law does not apply, where Somali officials may not enter and where Somali customs cannot examine what arrives would no longer be Somali in any meaningful sense. Every state insists on knowing what crosses its territory. Commercial goods have nothing to fear from inspection. Cargo that must be hidden from the hostcountry is, by definition, something other than ordinary trade, and it has no place on Somali soil. There is also an obligation that goes beyond national interest. Somalia, like Ethiopia, is a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and the Chemical Weapons Convention. UN Security Council Resolution 1540 requires every state to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and to control the transit of dangerous materials through its territory. A sealed enclave guarded by foreign troops would make it impossible for Somalia to meet those commitments. If anything harmful passed through such a zone, it would be Somalia that answered to the international community, for cargo it had never been permitted to see. Ethiopia has accepted the same treaty obligations and cannot reasonably ask a neighbour to set them aside. A diplomat with Rondos’s long experience of peace and security in the region understands these obligations well. To propose an uninspected sovereign enclave in one of the world’s most fragile regions is not responsible advice, and it should be challenged. Nor is this a theoretical concern. Ethiopia has already pursued similar terms elsewhere. In April, Djibouti’s ports authority said it had offered Ethiopia a 60 per cent share in the port of Tadjoura, and that Ethiopia declined, seeking a corridor on top of the equity stake. In September, President Guelleh formally turned down an Ethiopian proposal for a corridor with extraterritorial rights stretching from the border to Tadjoura, together with an Ethiopian naval base. A majority stake in a working port was not enough for Addis Ababa. It wanted land, extraterritorial rights and a naval presence, which is precisely the necklace Rondos describes. Djibouti was able to refuse because it spoke with a single voice. Somalia should ask whether it could do the same. Its federal government and member states frequently pull in opposite directions; politicians compete for foreign patronage; clan rivalries continue to be turned against the national interest. The memorandum of understanding Ethiopia signed with Somaliland in January 2024, offering sea access in return for recognition, showed how readily a divided country can be negotiated with one region at a time. Ethiopia’s governments have changed many times since the era of Emperor Menelik, but the ambition for a coastline has remained constant. Where a united Djibouti could say no, a fragmented Somalia risks answering with many voices, and there will usually be someone prepared to say yes. This is why the warning matters most to younger Somalis, who will inherit whatever is agreed in their name. They should know this history, follow closely what is being negotiated, and hold every leader, federal and regional, to a clear standard. Ethiopia may have commercial access to Somali ports: open, subject to inspection and governed by Somali law. It may not have sovereign territory, foreign troops or uninspected cargo on the Somali coast, whether by agreement, for any price or in perpetuity. Somalis have united before when their land was under threat. They should not wait for another crisis to do so again. National reconciliation is now a matter of national security. A united Somalia would leave no opening to exploit, and would leave Ethiopia with a single realistic course: a fair commercial partnership that serves both countries and supports lasting stability in the Horn of Africa. __________________________________ Hussein Soyan is a former Somali head of mission to Algeria, and a political analyst, lecturer and social finance expert. somalia.summary: Somalia must firmly reject Ethiopia's proposal for a "necklace of ports," which would effectively transfer Somali territory to Ethiopian control. While Ethiopia's need for sea access is acknowledged, the idea of granting Ethiopia sovereign zones on Somali soil, as suggested by former EU representative Alexander Rondos, poses significant risks. Such zones would allow Ethiopia to operate without Somali oversight, undermining Somalia's sovereignty and international obligations under treaties like the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The article emphasizes that Somalia's fragmented political landscape could lead to dangerous concessions, as seen in Ethiopia's previous negotiations with Djibouti and Somaliland. The call for national reconciliation is framed as a matter of national security, urging Somalis to unite against external pressures and negotiate fair partnerships that promote stability in the Horn of Africa.

football.title: ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ - winwin
football.content: ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ لاعبو الفريق الرديف بنادي الهلال السوداني (Facebook/ Al Hilal S.C) 22 نوفمبر 2026 ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أحدثت إدارة نادي الهلال السوداني ثورة تغيير مفاجئة بإطاحتها بالطاقم الفني للفريق الرديف قبل أيام قليلة من انطلاقة النسخة الحادية والثلاثين من مسابقة الدوري السوداني الممتاز، إذ يفتتح الفريق مسيرته يوم الأربعاء 25 نوفمبر على ملعب مدينة كريمة. وأبدت إدارة النادي جرأة كبيرة وثقة في قدرة الفريق على تجاوز توقيت هذا القرار الحساس، محددة أهدافها بوضوح دون الالتفات لردود الفعل الجماهيرية. لا سيما بعد أن استقرت على قرار المشاركة بالفريق الرديف في المرحلة الأولى للنسخة 31 من مسابقة الدوري. أسباب إقالة الجهاز الفني لرديف الهلال السوداني وكشفت مصادر موثوقة لموقع " winwin " أنّ إدارة العملاق السوداني استهدفت التطوير، خاصة بعد الأداء المتواضع الذي ظهر به الفريق خلال معسكره التحضيري في العاصمة الرواندية "كيغالي"، إضافةً إلى فشل المدرب النيجيري نور الدين أويرورو في تقديم ما يبرر استمراره، لا سيما أن الهدف من التعاقد معه كان بناء فريق للمستقبل، وهو ما أكدته التقارير السلبية للجنة الفنية المختصة، مما دفع الإدارة لاتخاذ هذا القرار السريع قبل بدء الاستحقاقات المحلية، فيما كانت قد فضلت إكمال اتفاقها مع المدرب الفرنسي ألكسندر لافيت قبل أن تعلن عن إقالة أويرورو وكافة أفراد طاقمه المعاون بمن فيهم المدرب المحلي محمد عطا. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يقيل أويرورو ويعين مدربا فرنسيا خلفا له الهلال يخطف فوزًا ثمينًا من البوليس ويقترب من صدارة الدوري الرواندي واتخذت الإدارة قرار تغيير الجهاز الفني دون النظر إلى التوقيت، في ظل ضعف مستوى أندية الدوري الممتاز، إلى جانب جاهزية الفريق ونجومه وثقة الإدارة في قدرة الطاقم الفني سواء كان محليًا أو أجنبيًا على تجاوز المرحلة الأولى من المسابقة. وقد حرصت إدارة الهلال السوداني على إعداد الفريق الرديف عبر معسكر تجريبي طويل خاض خلاله مباريات ودية قوية، وعززت صفوفه بنخبة من النجوم والمحترفين الأجانب لضمان تأهله إلى المرحلة الختامية من المسابقة التي سيشارك فيها الفريق الأول. وسيستهل بطل الدوري الممتاز مشواره بمواجهة قوية أمام الأهلي مروي يوم الأربعاء 25 نوفمبر على ملعب مدينة كريمة الأولمبي، علمًا بأنّ الفريق ينافس ضمن المجموعة الثانية التي تضم كلا من: الأهلي مروي، هلال كريمة، السهم الدامر، الفلاح عطبرة، الأمل عطبرة، الرابطة السليم، والأمير دنقلا. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات football.summary: أحدثت إدارة نادي الهلال السوداني تغييرات جذرية بإقالة الطاقم الفني للفريق الرديف قبل أيام من انطلاق الدوري السوداني الممتاز. يأتي هذا القرار بعد الأداء المخيب الذي قدمه الفريق خلال معسكره التحضيري في كيغالي، حيث فشل المدرب النيجيري نور الدين أويرورو في تحقيق الأهداف المرجوة. الإدارة، التي أظهرت جرأة وثقة في قدرتها على تجاوز هذا التوقيت الحساس، قررت الاستعانة بالمدرب الفرنسي ألكسندر لافيت. كما أكدت الإدارة على أهمية تطوير الفريق الرديف، الذي سيشارك في المرحلة الأولى من الدوري، حيث تم تعزيز صفوفه بنجوم محترفين. الهلال سيبدأ مشواره في الدوري بمواجهة الأهلي مروي يوم 25 نوفمبر، ضمن مجموعة تضم عدة أندية. هذه الخطوات تعكس رغبة الإدارة في تحسين الأداء وتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المنافسات المحلية.

football.summary: استعد فريق النجم الساحلي لمباراته المرتقبة ضد الهلال السوداني في إطار منافسات دوري أبطال إفريقيا. شهدت التدريبات الأخيرة تركيزًا كبيرًا من اللاعبين والجهاز الفني، حيث تم العمل على تعزيز الجوانب الفنية والبدنية. كما تم إجراء تقييم شامل للاعبين من حيث اللياقة البدنية والتكتيك، لضمان جاهزيتهم التامة للمباراة. يهدف النجم الساحلي إلى تحقيق نتيجة إيجابية في هذه المواجهة الهامة، حيث تعتبر المباراة فرصة لتعزيز موقف الفريق في البطولة. يتطلع المدرب إلى استغلال نقاط القوة لدى لاعبيه، مع الأخذ بعين الاعتبار أسلوب لعب الهلال السوداني. من المتوقع أن تشهد المباراة تنافسًا قويًا، حيث يسعى كلا الفريقين لتحقيق الفوز. الجماهير أيضًا متحمسة لدعم فريقها في هذه المباراة الحاسمة.

مباراتيه أمام الهلال السوداني وحوريا كوناكري الغيني، برسم دور مجموعات عصبة الأبطال الإفريقية، فيما لا يزال مصير المواجهة المرتقبة أمام بيراميدز المصري يلفه الغموض، سواء من حيث الملعب المحتضن أو موعد إجرائها. وقررت إدارة «الماص» استقبال الهلال السوداني وحوريا كوناكري على أرضية الملعب الشرفي بمكناس، حيث سيكون الفريق الفاسي على موعد مع أول ظهور قاري له بالمدينة يوم 5 دجنبر المقبل، عندما يواجه الهلال السوداني لحساب الجولة الثانية من دور المجموعات. كما سيستقبل المغرب الفاسي فريق حوريا كوناكري يوم 19 دجنبر، ضمن الجولة الثالثة، في مواجهتين يراهن عليهما ممثل الكرة المغربية لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية وجمع نقاط ثمينة تعزز حظوظه في بلوغ الأدوار الإقصائية من المسابقة القارية. في المقابل، لا يزال الملعب الذي سيحتضن مباراة المغرب الفاسي أمام بيراميدز المصري، برسم الجولة الخامسة، غير محسوم إلى حدود الساعة، كما لم يتم الإعلان رسميا عن موعد إجرائها، في انتظار استكمال المشاورات والترتيبات الإدارية والأمنية المرتبطة بتنظيم هذه المواجهة. هذا ومن المنتظر أن يحتضن الملعب الشرفي بمكناس مباريات المغرب الفاسي على غرار مبارياته في البطولة بحضور جماهيره في حالة موافقة السلطات، في انتظار انتهاء الأشغال الجارية بملعب الحسن الثاني بمدينة فاس. جميع الحقوق محفوظـة © المرجو عند نقل المقال، ذكر المصدر الأصلي للموضوع مع football.summary: قرر نادي المغرب الرياضي الفاسي استضافة مباراتيه في دور مجموعات عصبة الأبطال الإفريقية على الملعب الشرفي بمكناس. ستقام المباراة الأولى ضد الهلال السوداني في 5 دجنبر، تليها مواجهة مع فريق حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 19 دجنبر. يسعى الفريق الفاسي لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في هاتين المباراتين لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل للأدوار الإقصائية. ومع ذلك، لا يزال مصير المباراة المرتقبة أمام بيراميدز المصري غير محدد، حيث لم يتم الإعلان عن الملعب أو موعد إجرائها بعد، في انتظار استكمال الترتيبات اللازمة. يُذكر أن الملعب الشرفي بمكناس سيستضيف أيضًا مباريات المغرب الفاسي في البطولة الوطنية، وذلك في حال حصول الفريق على موافقة السلطات، خاصةً في ظل الأعمال الجارية بملعب الحسن الثاني في فاس.
